title: What Is the Failure Rate of House Flippers? The Real Numbers You Need to Know
excerpt: Most new house flippers lose money on their first deal — but the reasons why are predictable and avoidable. Here's what the data says about flip failure rates and how smart investors beat the odds.
author: AIWholesail Team
metaDescription: What is the failure rate of house flippers? Learn the real statistics, top reasons flips fail, and proven strategies to protect your profits on every deal.

sections.content: If you've ever watched a house-flipping show on TV, it looks easy. Buy a run-down house, fix it up in six weeks, and walk away with a $60,000 check. The reality is quite different. So what is the failure rate of house flippers, really? Studies and industry data suggest that roughly 40% of first-time house flippers lose money on their initial deal. Some estimates put the broader failure rate — meaning flippers who quit after one or two deals — as high as 70% within the first two years. That's a sobering number, but it's also one you can beat if you understand what's going wrong for everyone else.
What Does 'Failure' Actually Mean for a House Flipper?

Before diving into the numbers, it helps to define what failure looks like in this business. Some flippers lose money outright — they sell the property for less than what they put into it. Others break even but forget to account for their time, carrying costs, and opportunity costs. And a third group makes a small profit on the sale but never flips again because the process was too stressful, too slow, or too unpredictable. All three scenarios count as a failure to build a sustainable flipping business. When researchers and industry analysts talk about the failure rate of house flippers, they're usually grouping all three of these outcomes together.
The Real Numbers Behind House Flipping Failure

ATTOM Data Solutions, which tracks real estate trends across the U.S., found that the average gross profit on a flip was around $67,900 in recent years — but gross profit is not the same as net profit. Once you subtract renovation costs, financing fees, real estate commissions (typically 5-6%), holding costs like property taxes and utilities, and closing costs, many flippers are left with far less than they expected. In competitive markets, some deals end in a net loss. A house flipper who buys at the wrong price, underestimates rehab costs, or holds a property for six months longer than planned can quickly see a $30,000 projected profit turn into a $10,000 loss.
'In real estate flipping, it's not the market that kills most investors — it's the spreadsheet they never built before they bought.' — Common wisdom among experienced real estate investors
Top 6 Reasons House Flippers Fail

items: Overpaying for the property: Failing to correctly calculate the After Repair Value (ARV) leads investors to offer too much on the front end, leaving no room for profit.
Underestimating renovation costs: Surprise expenses — like foundation issues, outdated electrical, or hidden mold — regularly blow up budgets by 20-40%.
Poor contractor management: Delays from unreliable contractors extend holding costs by weeks or months, draining profit on every extra day you own the property.
Ignoring carrying costs: Mortgage interest, insurance, property taxes, and utilities can run $2,000-$5,000 per month on a typical flip. A 3-month delay costs $6,000-$15,000 in costs alone.

Buying in the wrong market: Flipping in a slow or declining market means your ARV assumptions may be wrong by the time you list. Active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) move faster and offer better exit options.
Lack of a backup exit strategy: Flippers who can't sell quickly sometimes have no plan B — no option to rent, wholesale, or hold. This leaves them forced to drop the price dramatically just to close.

sections.content: How Successful Flippers Beat the Odds
They Run the Numbers Before Making an Offer

Experienced flippers don't fall in love with a property before they've modeled the deal. They start with ARV, work backward using the 70% rule (meaning they won't pay more than 70% of ARV minus repair costs), and only move forward when the numbers genuinely work. This sounds obvious, but emotional buying is one of the most common mistakes new investors make. Before you ever call a contractor, you need a reliable rehab estimate. Tools like the free [Rehab Estimator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator) can help you quickly scope out likely renovation costs by property type and condition, so you're not guessing when you sit down to structure your offer.
They Build a Reliable Contractor Network

Ask any seasoned flipper what their most valuable asset is, and most will say their contractor. A good general contractor who shows up on time, stays on budget, and communicates daily is worth their weight in gold. The best way to find reliable contractors is through referrals from other investors in your local market. Join your local real estate investment association (REIA), attend meetups, and ask who other flippers are using. Vet every contractor by checking references, pulling their license, and confirming they carry liability insurance before handing over a single dollar.
They Know Their Market Inside and Out

Flippers who succeed long-term often specialize in a specific neighborhood or zip code. They know which streets sell fast, which school districts drive buyer demand, and how much buyers will actually pay for upgraded kitchens versus standard finishes. This local knowledge lets them buy smarter and renovate smarter. If you're new to a market, spend 60-90 days studying comps before you buy anything. Drive neighborhoods, attend open houses, and talk to local agents about what buyers are looking for right now.

Pro Tip: Always add a 15-20% contingency buffer on top of your contractor's estimate before you finalize your offer price. Hidden costs on renovations are the rule, not the exception — especially in older homes built before 1980.
Alternatives If Flipping Feels Too Risky Right Now

Flipping isn't the only way to profit in real estate. If the failure rate of house flippers has you second-guessing your strategy, there are lower-risk entry points worth considering. Wholesaling, for example, lets you find discounted properties and assign the contract to another buyer — earning an assignment fee without ever owning the property or managing a renovation. Can You Reduce Your Risk as a New Flipper?

Absolutely. The failure rate of house flippers is high, but it is not random. Most flippers fail because of decisions made before the purchase, not because of bad luck. Here's a simplified checklist to reduce your risk on every deal:

items: Confirm your ARV using at least 3-5 sold comps from the past 90 days within a half-mile of your property.
Get two to three contractor bids before finalizing your numbers — never rely on just one estimate.
Calculate your total carrying costs for a realistic timeline, then add 30% more time as a buffer.
Identify your exit strategy before you buy: flip, rent, or wholesale.
Run every deal through a profit calculator that accounts for purchase price, rehab, financing, commissions, and taxes.
Start with one deal at a time until you have a repeatable system and a team you trust.

sections.content: The investors who succeed long-term treat flipping like a business with documented processes, not a side hustle they wing deal by deal. They track their numbers religiously, learn from every mistake, and constantly improve their buying criteria and contractor relationships. The gap between a 40% failure rate and consistent profitability usually comes down to preparation, not talent.
